newsitem.title: CHINA: Philippines on course despite soft peso-M.Grenfell.
newsitem.headline: Philippines on course despite soft peso-M.Grenfell.

text.p: Despite recent currency woes, the Philippines stands to benefit from a rating upgrade, lower borrowing costs and good fundamentals, bankers said on Monday.

"We believe that the Philippines will be upgraded in the next 12 months," Eammon McConnell, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell managing director and head of global markets syndicate, Asia, told a bond conference.

The Philippines carries a BB-plus long-term foreign-currency rating from Standard & Poor's, and Moody's Investors Service rates its foreign-currency bonds and notes Ba1 and its long-term bank deposits Ba2.
McConnell cited the falling cost of funds for good Philippine issuers like Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co (PLDT) as an example.

"It's a very frequent issuer to the market. In 1994, it paid 350 basis points over the 10-year (U.S. Treasury). In 1995, it was 340 (basis points), in 1996, it was 240 (basis points), and in 1997 ... 150 (basis points)," McConnell said.
After the Philippines's sovereign rating was investment grade, it could tap "a new pool" of funds, and the era of investors demanding top rates had already ended, he said.
"Clearly, the easy money is over -- buying PLDT (debt paper) at Treasuries plus 350," McConnell said.
Angus Armstrong, chief economist with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, praised the economic track record of Philippines president Fidel Ramos as "extremely impressive".
Referring to the Philippines' central bank's track record in recent years, Armstrong said: "We think the central bank actually has done a very good job".
But he criticised the record of Philippine commercial banks for using foreign deposits to fund domestic loans.

In a conference at which comparisons of Thailand and the Philippines have been a recurrent theme, Armstrong said Philippine banks had to hedge foreign exchange exposure, so were in better shape than their Thai counterparts.
Armstrong said problems rising from attacks on the peso and from a central bank decision to let the peso move in a wider band, would not hurt longer term economic performance.
He said a managed float, in which the peso moved in a band, rather than a fixed float would stop people from borrowing foreign currency thinking they were safe from volatility.
